summary: Defines a DHCPv6 option that lets a home or office router learn which IPv4-over-IPv6 tunneling method (softwire) its provider prefers. This lets one device support several competing approaches and pick the right one.

eli5.summary: Your provider speaks only a new language but you need to reach old-language sites. This lets your router ask which translation trick to use, so one box works with many.

questions: what is the dhcpv6 s46 priority option
how does a cpe choose between map-e and ds-lite
subtitle: A DHCPv6 option that tells a router which IPv4-over-IPv6 method to prefer when several are offered.

tldr.problem: Providers moving to IPv6 have several ways to carry IPv4 inside IPv6, and a single home router may support more than one and receive configuration for several at once.
tldr.mechanism: A new DHCPv6 option, OPTION_S46_PRIORITY (code 111), lists the option codes of the mechanisms in priority order, and the router configures the first listed mechanism it was actually provisioned for.
tldr.outcome: One router can work across providers and during migrations between mechanisms, with no extra server-side logic. It does not provide fallback if the chosen mechanism fails.

facts.label: Option length
facts.value: At least 2, a multiple of 2 octets

today: RFC 8026 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the S46 Priority Option and its IANA registry.

sections.title: Why Softwire Clients Need a Priority List
sections.content:
IPv4 service continuity is a major challenge during IPv6 migration. Several approaches carry IPv4 packets inside IPv6 across an IPv6-only provider network. The RFC calls them S46 mechanisms. Examples named in the text are DS-Lite (RFC 6333), Lightweight 4over6 (RFC 7596), MAP-E (RFC 7597) and MAP-T (RFC 7599).

All of them put a tunnel endpoint in the Customer Premises Equipment (CPE) router, so one CPE may be able to support several. A provider may also run more than one mechanism at once, for example during a migration. For this to work, the CPE and the provider need a way to say which mode is preferred.
sections.eli5: There are several secret tunnels from your house to the old internet, and your router knows how to use more than one. It needs to be told which tunnel to pick first.

sections.title: Design Goals
sections.content:
The RFC lists seven rationale points. The main ones are smooth migration paths between mechanisms, deterministic behavior when several mechanisms coexist in the CPE or in the provider network, and reuse of shared building blocks such as tunnel endpoints and the port-restricted NAPT44.

It also wants solution-agnostic wording, flexibility for operators to compile CPE software only for the modes they need, and simplicity. The method needs no server-side logic and only a simple prioritization step in the CPE.
sections.eli5: The goal is one box that works for many providers, is easy to predict, and does not need extra parts you will never use.

sections.title: The S46 Priority Option
sections.content:
The option has the code OPTION_S46_PRIORITY (111) and an option-length that is at least 2 and a multiple of 2 octets. The rest is a list of 16-bit s46-option-code values. Each one is the registered DHCPv6 option code that identifies a softwire mechanism, and the order in the option is the priority order.

The option MUST contain at least one code. If a client sees the same code more than once, it should treat the option as invalid. Servers MAY check the list for invalid values and duplicates. The option is a singleton, so servers MUST NOT send more than one instance.
sections.eli5: It is a ranked list of numbers, where each number stands for one tunnel type. The first number is the favorite. Writing the same number twice makes the list broken.

sections.title: Client Behavior
sections.content:
A client MAY ask for the option by listing it in its Option Request Option. When an Advertise message arrives containing the priority option, the client does four things:

  1. Builds a candidate list of S46 mechanisms from the valid configuration options in the message.
  2. Builds a priority list from the codes in OPTION_S46_PRIORITY, highest first.
  3. Walks the priority list until an entry matches the candidate list.
  4. Configures that mechanism (it MUST do so).

If nothing matches, the client MAY configure one or more of the provisioned mechanisms, and which ones is left to the implementation. If the option is invalid, the client MAY behave as if it had not been received. A client MUST skip an unknown option code and keep going.
sections.eli5: The router checks its favorites list from the top and uses the first tunnel it actually has settings for. If none match, it may choose by itself.

sections.title: Deployment Advice for Operators
sections.content:
Reusing one IPv4 range across several mechanisms makes return traffic hard to route. A client using MAP-E may send through a MAP-E border relay while the return traffic reaches a MAP-T relay, and the translated packet is then dropped. The RFC advises separate IPv4 pools per mechanism. IPv6 client addresses may overlap if only one mechanism serves a client at a time, but the tunnel concentrator address (BR or AFTR) needs to differ for each mechanism.

Older clients that support several mechanisms but do not request the priority option may get configuration for all of them, which can be unpredictable. The operator may then need server logic to give such clients a single mechanism, at the cost of complexity and scalability.

The method is only a priority order. If the top mechanism stops working, switching to the next one is out of scope.
sections.eli5: If two tunnels share the same mailbox addresses, replies can end up at the wrong door. Give each tunnel its own set of addresses.

sections.title: IANA Registry and Security
sections.content:
IANA allocated DHCPv6 option code 111 and created a registry, "Option Codes permitted in the S46 Priority Option", with new entries added by IETF Review. The initial values are 64 (DS-Lite), 88 (DHCPv4 over DHCPv6), 94 (MAP-E), 95 (MAP-T) and 96 (Lightweight 4over6).

For security, the considerations of RFC 6334 and RFC 7598 apply. A misbehaving intermediate node could alter the option and steer the client to a different mechanism, or alter it along with other options so traffic is intercepted by an illegitimate node. The RFC notes this is true of any DHCPv6 option.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of which number means which tunnel. Someone sneaky in the middle could change the list, but that is true for any such note.

fields.name: option-length
fields.desc: At least 2 and a multiple of 2, in octets.
